before.supportingExcerpt: Variant-effect prediction estimates a specified consequence of a sequence change, whereas variant calling identifies changes from sequence data. Ensembl maps each allele of a variant onto every overlapping transcript with a rule-based approach, so the same genomic change can have a different consequence in different transcripts, and its impact categories (high, moderate, low, modifier) are qualitative assumptions about likely effect, not a measured loss of function (Ensembl documentation, release 116). A score from a missense tool does not answer a splice or regulatory question, and a prediction should name the reference genome, the alleles and the transcript (with its version) it was made for. A raw model score is not automatically a probability: a splice score of 0.92 on an unspecified scale does not mean a 92 per cent chance of lost function, because thresholds and evidence strengths belong to a particular tool and task. The absence of a prediction does not make a variant benign, because a tool may not cover that variant type or transcript. RNA junction evidence, functional experiments and clinical studies address different gaps, and none is interchangeable with a sequence score. Two reports of the same prediction from the same software version are two copies of one computed result, not two independent experiments. Where a tool's training data overlap the variants used to evaluate it, its performance can be overestimated, which is why the ClinGen calibration of thirteen missense tools to ACMG/AMP pathogenicity and benignity evidence strengths, estimated from local positive predictive value, used datasets assembled to minimise that circularity (Pejaver and colleagues, 2022). That calibration used ClinVar missense variants classified as pathogenic or benign and rare in gnomAD, within the ACMG/AMP recommendations for variants in genes associated with monogenic disease, and it selected no tool designed for splice variants. Its introduction notes that many methods overlap and so do not offer independent assessment of pathogenicity, which is why agreement between tools that share training data or inputs is not independent confirmation. The AMP, ASCO and CAP guideline for somatic variants notes that early prediction algorithms were developed and validated for germline variants and recommends that their results never be used as the sole evidence for variant classification or clinical decision making (Li and colleagues, 2017).
